title: Access in the justice system
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:38Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-02T04:41:51Z recheck: the fresh check agreed with the fix, cleared with the fix

match.reason: The bank point covers Indigenous over-representation in custody, while the new point teaches access to rights and to the justice system, so they are different ideas.

draft.title: Access in the justice system
card: Access means people can learn about their rights and use the justice system to protect them. It is one of the principles used to judge whether the system is working well.
People need information about their rights and how the system works. Plain language, community legal education and interpreters help people understand.
People also need to be able to take part. Cost, distance, language and a lack of legal help can all stand in the way.
Access is about being able to reach and use the system. It is not a promise of any particular result.
draft.remember: Access means knowing your rights and being able to use the system to protect them.

a.q: Which situation is mainly a problem of access to the justice system?
opts: A person cannot afford a lawyer to explain their options
A judge refuses to hear a person's side of the case
A person is treated differently from others for no reason
A court reaches a decision the person disagrees with
a.why: Not being able to pay for legal help can stop a person from using the system to protect their rights. A judge refusing to hear a side is about the fairness of the hearing, not access.
a.clue: Which one stops a person from getting into the system?

b.q: Tran has lived in Australia for one year and speaks little English. He has a legal problem but does not understand his rights. Which step would best improve his access?
opts: Free information and an interpreter in his own language
A rule that the court must decide in his favour
A faster hearing date than other people get
A ban on the other party using a lawyer
b.why: Information and an interpreter help Tran learn his rights and take part in the system. Access is not a promise of a result, so a rule that he must win does not improve access.
b.clue: Access is about knowing and using, not about winning.

a.best: A person cannot afford a lawyer to explain their options

b.best: Free information and an interpreter in his own language

problems.detail: The three wrong options (a rule that the court must rule for him, a faster hearing than others, a ban on the other party's lawyer) are plainly unreasonable, so a Year 12 student can pick the right answer without understanding access.

a.q: Which situation is mainly a problem of access to the justice system?
opts: A person cannot afford a lawyer to explain their options
A judge refuses to hear a person's side of the case
A person is treated differently from others for no reason

a.why: Not being able to pay for legal help can stop a person from using the system to protect their rights. A judge refusing to hear a side is about the fairness of the hearing, not access.

b.q: Tran has lived in Australia for one year and speaks little English. He has a legal problem but does not understand his rights. Which step would best improve his access?
opts: Free legal information and an interpreter in his language
A judge with no personal link to either party in the case
The same English court forms that every other party gets
A written statement of reasons after the case is decided
b.why: Tran's barriers are language and not knowing his rights, and information with an interpreter removes both. Giving him the same English forms as everyone else treats him alike but leaves the language barrier in place. An unbiased judge and written reasons concern the fairness of the hearing, not his ability to reach and use the system.
b.clue: Which step removes the barriers Tran actually faces?
